document_title: The Machine Makes Time. Who Owns the Clock?
post_copy:
On a Cook Inlet salmon boat this month, a sockeye enters a steel box on deck and leaves it iced.

Computer vision picks the fish and the path. Brain spiked, gills cut, iced, 6.5 seconds or less by Shinkei's count.

Upper Cook Inlet holds more than 1,300 drift and set gillnet permits, and sockeye carries the value there. Boats in that fleet now carry the machine. It goes aboard free. The catch reportedly sells at a premium. That deal is fair.

A suffocated salmon stiffens in about 7 hours. Shinkei says its process stretches that to 60. Those hours become a brand, Seremoni Grade, a 16,000 square foot plant in Tacoma, and NERA, the firm's own system rating how many days a fish can be sold. Headquarters is El Segundo.

Alaska holds the fish, the water and the crews. Who gets to decide where the clock is owned?

#CookInletSalmon #IkeJime #AlaskaSeafood

aftercare: Post Tuesday through Thursday, 8 to 11am Alaska time. If this morning's window closes, hold for the next morning rather than posting into the afternoon.
Upload the PDF as a document post and set the document title to The Machine Makes Time. Who Owns the Clock? exactly. LinkedIn will not let you change it after publishing.
Paste the first-comment source block within 60 seconds of publishing, then reload and confirm every URL rendered as visible full text.
Reply substantively to every comment in the first 90 minutes. Threaded author replies are the largest reach lever available and a dead first hour is rarely recovered.

If a permit holder, a processor or a Shinkei employee corrects the split, the boat count or the premium, thank them, ask one follow-up, and send the correction back into the run notes. Do not argue the thesis in the thread.
At 48 hours log saves and comments against the trailing median, weighting saves over comments over shares over likes.
